subtopic: STATEMENT ON COMMUNITY ANTENNA SYSTEMS

speakeroldname: Hon. J. W. Pickersgill (Minister of Transport):
subtopic: STATEMENT ON COMMUNITY ANTENNA SYSTEMS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to make a statement on community antenna television broadcasting. In a statement on December 31, 1963, the Minister of Transport and the Secretary of State indicated that for some time the problem of the effect of community antenna television on national broadcasting policy had been of concern to the government.
In order to give the government an opportunity to consider the problem it was announced on December 31 that until further notice no new licences or amendments to existing licences would be approved for CATV installations to receive and disseminate programs emanating from broadcasting stations outside Canada. It was also decided that no new or amended licences would be granted to any applicant in any case where more than 25 per cent of the ownership of the installation was held by persons who are not citizens of Canada, in the same way as licences for television broadcasting are limited by the Broadcasting Act. This ownership requirement was confirmed by an interim ministerial order issued by the Minister of Transport on February 21, 1964.
The government asked the board of broadcast governors, in consultation with the technical experts of the Department of Transport, to inquire into and recommend any legislative action which might be required to ensure that, so far as the constitutional jurisdiction of parliament would permit, the use of community antenna television for the dissemination of television programs was subject to similar regulation under parallel conditions to that applied to broadcasting.
The report was received by the government on March 9, 1964 and was tabled in the house. Since that date the government has received representations from the national community antenna television association of Canada and given prolonged study to the problems involved.
The government has two main concerns. One is to see that CATV installations in Canada do not come under the ownership and control of persons and corporations which are not Canadian. The other is to see that CATV installations designed to receive broadcasts emanating from outside the area reached by any local Canadian television station, and particularly from outside Canada, are unlikely to make the operation of any existing television station uneconomic or to inhibit the provision of alternate Canadian television service in the area concerned.
So far as ownership is concerned, it has been found that the interim ministerial order of February 21 does not ensure an effective degree of Canadian ownership and control of CATV installations. It is proposed therefore to amend the order of the Minister of Transport so as to ensure effective Canadian ownership and control of new CATV installations. A draft of the proposed amending order is being tabled now. It will come into effect on August 1, and will apply only to new installations or to changes proposed for the first time after today in the ownership of existing installations. Applications already before the department will be considered on their individual merits as was the case before December 31, 1963.
The so-called freeze will be lifted immediately and the Minister of Transport will deal with pending applications after informal consultation with the board of broadcast governors on the possible effect on television broadcasting in the area concerned. Since there is some doubt as to the power of the board of broadcast governors to hold hearings, the government proposes to ask parliament, through approval of an item in the next supplementary estimates of the Department of Transport, to clothe the board with the necessary authority to hold such hearings pending a more formal amendment of the Broadcasting Act or the Radio Act. Meanwhile the Minister of Transport will, in the exercise of his powers under the Radio Act, content himself with informal consultation with the board of broadcast governors.
In announcing the lifting of the so-called freeze the government wishes to emphasize that it has no desire to regulate CATV for

Community Antennae Broadcasting the sake of regulation, but merely to the minimum extent deemed necessary to maintain the Canadian identity and character of broadcasting to the greatest extent practicable, in accord with the consistent position taken by all governments and parliaments since the Aird report of 1929.
Now, sir, I have for tabling what the government proposes as an item in the next supplementary estimates and what I propose to make as a ministerial order with regard to ownership. Possibly it would be very boring if I were to read these documents, and it might be convenient for hon. members either to have them printed as an appendix to Hansard or perhaps, in these very unusual circumstances, they might just follow my statement and be deemed to have been read, so they would all be in one place in Hansard-

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am sure the house and all hon. members will appreciate having this statement from the Minister of Transport concerning the CATV operators throughout Canada. We are pleased to know that the freeze has been lifted. I am sure this will be well

received by those in the industry because it has created a great hardship on this industry since December 31, 1963, when this freeze was placed on the operators of CATV outlets.
The minister states that he is primarily concerned with the ownership of these operations, and I do not think we have any complaints in this regard. With respect to the other matter concerning the regulations relating to CATV, it remains to be seen what the Department of Transport will do in this connection. I understood the minister to say that interviews will be afforded these people in the industry, so we will just have to wait and see what is the outcome of these hearings which the minister proposes. But we are certainly pleased that this freeze has been lifted, and we will await further developments.

subtopic: STATEMENT ON COMMUNITY ANTENNA SYSTEMS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the weakness in the government policy that has just been announced is that it is impossible to go back and clear up the situation where CATV systems are already in existence, and affecting the existing stations. They are in existence and are providing a service, particularly on United States channels. With the introduction of this new policy it seems to me that this kind of development would block them off from other areas of the country. It is obvious that this is an inequity in that parts of the country which might have looked forward to the kind of service which, for example, Port Arthur has but which Sault Ste. Marie or Wawa has not, will be inhibited by this new policy. It is obvious that in this policy the minister has steered away from giving any firm indication of the government's reaction to the kind of regulation and control in this area that the board of broadcast governors set out in its last annual report it would wish.
I appreciate the reasons for this. We are in a kind of interim period until the matter is resolved. I suppose the solution which has been offered through this item in the supplementary estimates will look after the question of the hearings and the advice which will be sent forward from the board of broadcast governors to the Department of Transport radio department. But I suggest it does almost nothing to indicate whether the board is eventually going to have these powers, or whether the government feels that it should take care of the interests of the existing stations which are now transmitting and which are affected by CATV stations.
We welcome the announcement with regard to the ownership provision. It has been quite apparent that the major worry of many
Community Antennae Broadcasting of us about this CATV set-up becoming a network is that it is actually attracting and has attracted Famous Players Corporation, which is again a United States owned organization. We hope that this ownership organization will steer off expansion in that direction.
We welcome the fact that the freeze has ended. I suggest that this announcement by the government does not end the CATV problem, but that it will be with us for quite a number of years; and I think it will give rise to a great deal of bitterness of debate in this house and in parliamentary caucuses.

subtopic: STATEMENT ON COMMUNITY ANTENNA SYSTEMS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we welcome the announcement which has been made today. There has been a great deal of uncertainty in the minds of those interested in this particular matter throughout the past several months.
The question was raised as to whether there was any legal authority for intervention in this way, in imposing the freeze and then for the long delay occasioned since that time in order that it might be considered. All these things have created a great deal of uncertainty and dissatisfaction in the industry, but now that the minister has announced the freeze is being lifted it will alleviate the situation to a certain extent.
There has been a great fear in the minds of many residents of Canada that they were going to be deprived of services and privileges that those who live along the United States border are presently enjoying with the many channels available to them, while those living in areas further away from it are limited to one or two. The minister has announced that consideration will be given to the applications already made, and we hope that consideration will be favourable.

subtopic: REQUEST FOR COAT OF ARMS FOR MASSEY FAMILY
REQUEST FOR COAT OF ARMS FOR MASSEY FAMILY
speechtext:
1.	Did the government receive an application from Right Hon. Vincent Massey during 1962 or 1963 to be granted a coat of arms, with the crown thereon, for the use of Mr. Massey and his descendants to indicate that a member of the family had been the Queen's representative in Canada?
2.	If so, did the Prime Minister or the government of Canada submit such request to Her Majesty?
3.	Has the government received a reply to the said submission and, if so, what was the date and nature of such reply?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Prime Minister
subtopic: REQUEST FOR COAT OF ARMS FOR MASSEY FAMILY
speechtext:
1, 2 and 3. Mr. Massey's personal arms were granted by the College of

Arms in 1952. In 1961 the master of Massey College, University of Toronto, asked the College of Arms whether it would be possible to have some device added to Mr. Massey's personal arms which would allude to Mr. Massey's service to the crown as governor general of Canada. Mr. Massey's arms, thus modified, would serve as the arms and common seal of Massey College. The Garter King of Arms suggested that the logical course would be to seek an honourable augmentation of the arms of Mr. Massey himself, which might then be repeated in the college arms. Accordingly the master of Massey College made a request to the Governor General, who in turn consulted the ministry. On July 9, 1963, the Prime Minister advised the Governor General that the government concurred in the augmentation of Mr. Massey's arms in the manner proposed by the Garter King of Arms, namely that the augmentation should consist of "a canton azure charged with the crest of Canada a lion passant guardant or imperially crowned proper and holding in the dexter paw a maple leaf gules charged on the shield of Mr. Massey's arms in dexter chief". The warrant augmenting Mr. Massey's arms was signed by Her Majesty the Queen in October 1963 and countersigned by the Secretary of State of Canada in November 1963.
An augmentation of arms is a grant by the sovereign of an addition to a family coat of arms to mark some honourable achievement, the addition often being some part of the royal arms or badges.

speechtext:
1. The Department of Industry works with provincial departments in a number of fields in addition to those pertaining to designated areas. For example, various provincial departments have requested assistance in obtaining information on a variety of technical and industrial matters. The Department of Industry has been able, in most instances, to obtain and supply the information requested. In other cases, provincial departments have asked for assistance in dealing with specific industrial problems. The department has made staff available to co-operate with the provinces in attempting to find solutions to these problems. In other cases, provincial departments have asked for assistance from the department in appraising new production opportunities relating to local industries. This help has been forthcoming. A number of industry seminars have been jointly sponsored by provincial authorities and the Department of Industry with a view to fostering greater efficiency in industry.
2. As a rule, the Department of Industry does not work directly with municipalities or industrial commissioners. Direct liaison with municipal agencies respecting industrial development matters is usually the responsibility of provincial governments. However, if a municipal body requests specific information of a type which is normally available to other business groups in Canada, we will certainly assist them.

speechtext:

A farm safety planning conference was held in Ottawa on April 14, 1964, under the auspices of the national safety league of Canada. I wish to offer the hon. lady my good wishes on the occasion of what I think is her second question asked in the house. Hon. members did ask yesterday that immediately on the conclusion of this meeting I should give a report, and I should like to advise the house as follows.
The report of the royal commission on health services, volume I, was discussed in a preliminary way. However, this is a very complex document with important program
5814	HOUSE OF
Inquiries of the Ministry and financial implications. As it was only-received one month ago, it was considered by all to be impractical to discuss the document in detail. All governments will be examining it intensively and I indicated, as did the Prime Minister earlier this afternoon, that our own analysis should be completed in time to present the general position of the federal government to a federal-provincial conference by the end of this year or early next year.
The hospital insurance arrangements were also discussed and there was general acceptance of the principle of the integration of mental hospitals and tuberculosis sanatoria into the general hospital system. However, I did point out that the financial implications would need to be reviewed within the framework of the proposed study of the tax structure. In the meantime I urged the provinces to go ahead with the functional integration of these hospitals into the general hospital pattern. A special federal-provincial committee will be set up immediately to work out uniform criteria for the inclusion of mental care under the principles which apply to the hospital insurance program.
The federal government also agreed to establish arrangements for the continuing study of factors in the hospital system affecting hospital costs, and the provincial ministers agreed to co-operate and participate in these arrangements.
The general health grants received strong support and it was recommended that they continue without significant change in the basic pattern. Certain internal changes were proposed, such as the consolidation of research under the public health research grant and the streamlining of administration. These are matters which I propose to proceed with.
The provincial ministers expressed concern over the continuation of the hospital construction grant and I asked them to provide detailed information with regard to the need for new construction and renovation in each of the particular provinces. There was also discussion on the program "Smoking and Health" and the proposed conference on mental retardation in October.

subtopic: MEASURE TO FACILITATE MAKING LOANS TO STUDENTS

speechtext:
The house resumed, from Tuesday, July 21, consideration in committee of Bill No. C-110, to facilitate the making of loans to students [DOT]-Mr. Gordon-Mr. Lamoureux in the chair.
On clause 2-Definitions.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: MEASURE TO FACILITATE MAKING LOANS TO STUDENTS
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, when we rose last evening we were discussing the proposed amendment to clause 2(b) of the bill, and I think it might be of some assistance to the committee if I made a statement about this, which would help to put the structure of the bill into somewhat better perspective.
The discussion in connection with the amendment turns on the simple question, should the government of any province, that is the lieutenant governor in council, designate the provincial body or bodies which will lay down the provincial ground rules concerning universities and students, or should the federal government take the responsibility for designating the provincial body or bodies on the advice of the province. The government proposes the first of these two alternatives. Some members of the opposition parties have suggested the second, and I think it is not an oversimplification to say that the arguments used last night on both sides of the chamber were largely legal in nature.
An hon. member of the legal profession says that makes them all the stronger. I do not question that. All I am doing is making a statement. So far as the legal question is concerned I merely wish to restate today what I said last night, namely that I am prepared to take the responsibility, on behalf of the government, on the basis of the legal advice received from the government's advisers, that clause 2(b) is completely legal and in accord with precedent.
Moreover, I should like to emphasize we are quite satisfied that the functions that would devolve upon the provinces, that is upon the various lieutenant governors in council pursuant to clause 2(b), can be carried out by them without requiring further legislative action on the part of the provincial legislatures. Naturally if any of the provincial governments wish to obtain enabling legislation or believe this is necessary, then that is their privilege.
I listened to the debate last night, and yesterday afternoon, and the night before, and some periods before that, with very

great interest; and I must say I am impressed by the complexity and sophistication of the arguments advanced on both sides of the chamber concerning these legal and constitutional questions. As a layman I should like to speak for a few minutes in a non-legal vein and talk about the basic purposes which are germane not only to the specific clause now under discussion but to the bill as a whole as well, because I think the two are directly related.
In plain language this bill is designed to mobilize, on federal initiative and based on federal legislative powers, a large volume of financial resources to enable students to complete their higher education. It hopes and expects-and there is no reason to believe these hopes will be disappointed-that this will be done in collaboration with the provinces, and that the basic decisions outside of the strictly financial sphere will be made by the appropriate provincial bodies and not by the federal government.
Consequently this clause of the bill, along with various other clauses, makes it clear that the provinces, that is the lieutenant governors in council, will make the basic judgments as to which students, and which institutions and academic courses chosen by the students, are appropriate for financial assistance under the umbrella of this federal statute. It seems to me that a full appreciation of this point is crucial to a full understanding and appreciation of the legislation that is now before us.
Bill C-110 has been described as banking legislation, and rightly so. As we proceed with the further examination of the bill we will see that it is quite specific and quite authoritative on all essential points of a financial or banking nature, that is on all points relating to the granting of loans, the payment of interest and the repayment of loans.	.
The bill does not deal at all-and this is a very fundamental point, Mr. Chairman- with matters that might be construed to relate to the education of those who will benefit from the legislation. These are matters which we feel should be decided by the provinces, or by the authorities designated by the provinces. Hon. members will find that this view and intention is borne out in clause 13, dealing with the regulations. When we come to the paragraphs of clause 13 it will be found that virtually all of them relate strictly to matters of concern to the federal government and the banks.

I wish to say a few words on this amendment before a vote is taken. I think there is no point in labouring the subject at great length. We have made our position clear to the government. I had hoped the government and the Minister of Justice would have changed their minds, having had an opportunity to study the terms of the proposed amendment.
The point I wish to make is that we are not at variance with the Minister of Finance in what he is trying to do, but we take exception to the method he is adopting to bring about that end. We agree with the minister that the handling of student loans, the screening of applicants, the determination of what are educational institutions for the purposes of the act, can much better be done by the provincial authorities than by the federal government. This is why I suggested on second reading that it would be better if the federal government would agree to turn the actual funds over each year to the provincial student loans committees and let them handle the program. They have the machinery to do so, and the great advantage would be that those who were screening the applicants would be concerned mainly with getting them to university, not screening them, as bank managers are bound to do, on the basis of how the funds at the disposal of the bank can best be used.
But if the minister is not prepared to turn the actual funds over to the provincial governments to be administered by student loan committees, it seems to me that he has two alternatives. The one which this amendment proposes is very simple; that is, that the governor general in council should appoint these eligibility authorities, and they would accept the nominations of the provinces and

appoint the bodies that are already in existence in the provinces. But the appointments would be made by the governor general in council; they would be responsible to the governor general in council; they could be removed by the governor general in council, and they would be subject to regulation by the governor general in council.
There can be no argument about that being a sound proposition and the proper way in which to proceed. Instead, the government has taken what I think is a hybrid approach to the whole problem. It is going to be half and half; it is going to be banking legislation as far as the federal government is concerned, as far as guaranteeing the loans by the banks is concerned; but it is going to be provincial legislation in the matter of making the loans to the students and screening the applicants. Here we are going to have lieutenant governors in council, not just-as the parliamentary secretary to the Minister of Finance said-submitting to the governor general in council a schedule, or agenda or program for approval, but doing much more. We are giving to the lieutenant governor in council the power to appoint a body, with very wide discretionary powers, as one will find by reading clause (e) and the other clauses of the bill. The lieutenant governor in council has these wide discretionary powers that are not subject to control except in the matter of the form of the eligibility certificate. All the other provisions or regulations contained in clause 13 apply to the relationship with the banks.
The framework within which this eligibility authority will operate is not drafted and set out in the bill. The determination of what is a needy student, what is a student who can make good use of the money, what is a conscientious student, and all the criteria that are established is going to fall upon a committee over which the federal government has no control, a committee appointed by the lieutenant governor in council. These are very wide powers to give to a lieutenant governor in council. We are simply protesting this fact and saying, first, that it is a dangerous precedent to establish; and second, that the validity of this legislation could be called into question as a result of this provision.
We have made our protest. If the government, in spite of that protest, wants to blunder ahead and force this bill through, then I presume they can do so. The minister has never explained what objection there would be to the amendment and why it would not be just as satisfactory, and certainly

constitutionally much sounder, to have the governor general in council appoint these eligibility authorities. Then of course they could appoint whatever people the provinces recommended or whatever committees the provinces have already established. That would be simple. It seems to me it would be clear, beyond peradventure, if that procedure were followed. But if the minister does not want to accept the amendment, I would suggest that we take the vote and let us get on with the bill; because, while we do not consider that the legislation is of tremendous value, for those for whom it will have some value the sooner they get the advantages of it, the better. Therefore, Mr. Chairman, as far as we are concerned we will not belabour the matter any further and will give the committee a chance to vote on our amendment.

speechtext: The other way it could be done, Mr. Chairman, would be to have said that these co-operative lending institutions would be eligible to come under the act, provided they were incorporated under the laws of the province in which they were located. Because the kind of institution the minister mentions, like a small credit union with inadequate resources, would not be licensed under the laws of most provinces. However on the minister's assurance that this will be more or less a formal routine designation on application, I am quite prepared to go along with it.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: MEASURE TO FACILITATE MAKING LOANS TO STUDENTS
speechtext: I would be glad to give that assurance.

subtopic: MEASURE TO FACILITATE MAKING LOANS TO STUDENTS
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, on this particular point I should like to have some indication from the minister of the words "to be in need of a student loan", which are to be found in subparagraph (ii). I am concerned as to the criterion which the appropriate authority may use to determine what is the need for a student loan; what degree of uniformity and application there may be across the country. As I indicated in the debate yesterday, there can be great disparity in the application of this need as between provinces. Certainly under clause 13 the regulations go as to form; they do not go into

determination of what is need. I think we must get some assurance of uniform application.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: MEASURE TO FACILITATE MAKING LOANS TO STUDENTS
speechtext:
As I indicated a few minutes ago, Mr. Chairman, not only can I not give any such assurance but the whole structure and purpose of the bill is to leave those questions to the provincial authorities which will be administering these loans or issuing the certificates. As I said earlier, these bodies are in existence now. They have had a good deal of experience of this matter. There will be a quota for each province, so I do not think they will be extravagant in the way they exercise their authority in this regard.
I know of no effective way in which the federal government could act to ensure uniform criteria for need. As I said earlier, I think we will be relying on the experience, interest and good faith of the people who will be dealing with the students. They will be people who have dealt with them and are dealing with them now. I am quite certain that if in any one province it should happen that the authorized body was too tough with the students-I do not expect that would happen; after all, why should it?-the quotas are large enough so that the student could apply in another province if he wished to. After all, a man is resident anywhere in Canada wherever he happens to be, as I understand the law. But on the specific question put by the hon. member, I want to make it perfectly clear again that the structure of this bill is to leave questions of need, the kind of educational course, the kind of educational institution and that sort of question to the provincial body.

subtopic: MEASURE TO FACILITATE MAKING LOANS TO STUDENTS
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I hope I am not looking at this with an over jaundiced eye, but I can readily see where the designated authority could be in a position of not having to lend its own money in this particular instance. Let us assume that a student loan body in a province is lending provincial money, and as a result they are going to scrutinize the applications very carefully, particularly if they are made on the basis of need. In certain instances they might examine almost to the extent of finding out whether the parents have gold teeth, when the application is on the basis of need. Usually it is because the funds are more limited. I can readily see that a designated authority may say: "All right, we are going to save the province money; we will just shift this student over to the federal government". The purpose of the minister is to lend money to more

students; to make funds available to all students. If all that results is the transference of students from a provincial loan fund to this federal student loans scheme, nothing is being gained.
It is for this reason I rather suspect the minister is moving out into some shoals. After all, the bank manager in the usual course will be worried about the credit and other aspects of a loan. He is not concerned about the need for money, because he has a certificate. Somebody else has told him this student is in need of a loan of, say, $900. The appropriate body may say, "This young man said he needed $900." If this is a certificate of need, then I beg to differ with the minister.

subtopic: MEASURE TO FACILITATE MAKING LOANS TO STUDENTS
speechtext: I recognize that if we are going to leave this to the provincial bodies we cannot have uniformity across the country, but the certifying authorities have to have some framework within which to operate. There is nothing in clause 13 giving the governor in council power to make regulations to provide that framework. Will this be done by the lieutenant governors in council through provincial regulations, or does a certifying authority have to work out its own framework and modus operandi?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: MEASURE TO FACILITATE MAKING LOANS TO STUDENTS
speechtext: As I said, there are now provincial boards doing this, and have been doing it for some years. They are restricted in the amount of money available to them and there is no question in my mind that these people will do their best to see that loans are granted to students who need the money. With reference to the question of who needs the money, I think it was the hon. member for Edmonton West last night who was preaching the virtues of hardship and difficulty, and the fact that you got more out of education if you really had to struggle and sweat for it. He may be right, but the purpose of this bill is to make sure that if a student needs more money to get higher education at a university or in a vocational school, funds will be available to him to accomplish that end.

subtopic: MEASURE TO FACILITATE MAKING LOANS TO STUDENTS
speechtext: What the minister is really saying is that these certifying authorities will in all probability operate under the same regulations and terms of reference which they are operating under now.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: MEASURE TO FACILITATE MAKING LOANS TO STUDENTS
speechtext: That is right.

subtopic: MEASURE TO FACILITATE MAKING LOANS TO STUDENTS
speechtext:
Does the term "specified educational institution" cover an institution outside Canada?

subtopic: MEASURE TO FACILITATE MAKING LOANS TO STUDENTS
speechtext: What information can the minister give us with respect to the ceiling on loans of $1,000 a year? speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: MEASURE TO FACILITATE MAKING LOANS TO STUDENTS

subtopic: MEASURE TO FACILITATE MAKING LOANS TO STUDENTS
speechtext: With regard to specified institutions, will schools of nursing be included in the scope of the bill?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: MEASURE TO FACILITATE MAKING LOANS TO STUDENTS
speechtext: This, of course, is one of the things that will be up to the provinces to decide. As I said yesterday in answer to a question by the hon. member for York-Hum-ber, it seems to me nursing is a very important and essential profession and certainly it is the sort of thing this bill is intended to cover.

subtopic: MEASURE TO FACILITATE MAKING LOANS TO STUDENTS
speechtext: I was very interested in what the minister said a while ago, that the purpose of the bill is to give aid to whoever needed it for his or her education. If that is so, I ask the minister if any representations from the federal members for the province of Quebec have led him to take that course of not including or making these loans available to the province of Quebec?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: MEASURE TO FACILITATE MAKING LOANS TO STUDENTS
speechtext:
If I understand the hon. member correctly he wants to know what is the position of those members on this side of the chamber who come from the province of Quebec. I think I can assure him they are all strong supporters of the government in wishing to see this measure passed. So far as the question of making these loans available to students in Quebec is concerned, I have indicated that the government of the province has stated it would prefer to take advantage of clause 12 to handle its own plan itself, independently of the federal government. But if the government of the province of Quebec should find at any time that this plan had advantages and that it seemed attractive, the government of Quebec would

Loans to Students
be very welcome to change its mind and come in under this plan.

subtopic: MEASURE TO FACILITATE MAKING LOANS TO STUDENTS
speechtext: I thank the minister tor the explanation he has given me, but he has not succeeded in explaining how some members of the committee are in favour of one particular measure and on the other hand they do not take the necessary steps so that their compatriots can take advantage of it.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: MEASURE TO FACILITATE MAKING LOANS TO STUDENTS
speechtext: I cannot answer that question, except to remark that I have noticed some members of the party opposite have taken a view different from other members. I suppose it is a matter of individual choice.

subtopic: MEASURE TO FACILITATE MAKING LOANS TO STUDENTS
speechtext: If a student from one of the other provinces wishes to attend an educational institution in Quebec to whom does he apply for a loan? Would he apply in his own province? Further, would McGill University be certified as an institution in Alberta or British Columbia?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: MEASURE TO FACILITATE MAKING LOANS TO STUDENTS
speechtext: In that case he would apply in the province from which he was departing. I would point out that under the Quebec scheme their loan plans apply to Quebec students who wish to take their courses anywhere in Canada.

subtopic: MEASURE TO FACILITATE MAKING LOANS TO STUDENTS
speechtext:
In answer to the question by the hon. member for St. Hyacin-the-Bagot about the position of Liberal members of the committee from Quebec, I tell him we take our own responsibility.
When a vote comes we do not have to hide behind the curtain.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
subtopic: MEASURE TO FACILITATE MAKING LOANS TO STUDENTS
speechtext: Paragraph (g).

subtopic: MEASURE TO FACILITATE MAKING LOANS TO STUDENTS
speechtext: I have one question on paragraph (g). Would the minister kindly explain why the loan year is fixed from the 1st of July to the 30th of June in any calendar year? If this is primarily aimed at university education, it has been my experience that the academic year normally terminates about the 15th of May and starts about the 15th of September at the earliest. It may be that the true explanation is that in order to cover educational institutions other than universities it has been found preferable to use this term. I do not believe these loans may be used outside of the country, but if one were to attend the University of Oxford I could see it, because the school year terminates about the end of June.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: MEASURE TO FACILITATE MAKING LOANS TO STUDENTS
speechtext:
This is the point, Mr. Chairman. The end of the academic year varies from one institution to another. These loans

do apply to students who wish to attend a university in another country, including Oxford, I would presume. I think the hon. member has answered his own question.

subtopic: MEASURE TO FACILITATE MAKING LOANS TO STUDENTS
speechtext: I should like to ask a question for purposes of clarification. How long a period of post-student residence is required? What about the student who proceeds to postgraduate studies abroad? Let us say the student is the son of immigrant parents and he is in Canada for a period of four years while he takes an honours course, and then he is going to take a postgraduate course. He has had to sign a declaration that he intends to reside in Canada after he ceases to be a full time student. Is he still deemed to be a full time student if he goes on to a postgraduate course at some university outside the country where he may hold a fellowship or may be a research scholar? I realize these are very fine points but I assure the minister that as soon as the bill has been passed some postgraduate students are going to write to various members of parliament and put forward just this complicated type of question.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: MEASURE TO FACILITATE MAKING LOANS TO STUDENTS
speechtext:
If I may say so, I think the question is a very good one. As the hon. member suggests, the purpose of the clause is to make sure that children of new immigrants, which children have not yet acquired Canadian citizenship, are entitled to come in under the legislation. I am sure all hon. members will agree with that in principle. In the specific case to which my hon. friend refers the student in question, after four years or any other period here, would be entitled to go on and do postgraduate work in another country, as long as he indicated that it was his intention to come back here and reside in Canada.
I hope a lot of people will do this because it would be a good thing for them to do. I think one is entitled to ask: How do we know he is coming back? I believe there are two safeguards. First of all, I suggest that the great majority of people who take advantage of the scheme will live up to their obligations. Second, there is a limit to the amount of money that any individual can borrow.
Apart from that, it was my view when the legislation was being considered that if we tried to put too many strings on it we would put fences around people who proposed to benefit from an extra year or two of post-

graduate education anywhere in the world. This was something we wished to try to avoid.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subtopic: MEASURE TO FACILITATE MAKING LOANS TO STUDENTS
speechtext: I should like to ask a question with regard to the declaration of intention to reside in Canada. Suppose the person is not the child of immigrants but has come to Canada to study for a year and wants to remain, and then wants to return to his home country. Is there a limitation on this intention to reside? How long does the person have to reside in Canada? Is it the intention that he should become a Canadian citizen or that he should spend a year or two years here?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: MEASURE TO FACILITATE MAKING LOANS TO STUDENTS
speechtext: I do not think anybody who received a loan under this plan and who signed a certificate saying it was his intention to reside in Canada would feel he was living up to his obligation if he only stayed here for a couple of weeks after he graduated from university, and then left. On the other hand, I do not think anybody would wish to bind a student, who honestly intended to reside in Canada after his education was completed, to stay here for all time. There must be a certain amount of give and take.

subtopic: MEASURE TO FACILITATE MAKING LOANS TO STUDENTS
speechtext: I have a question which may be partly frivolous. Suppose a student has declared he intends to reside in Canada after having come here as a non-immigrant, but the immigration department does not approve of his intention to reside in Canada. Would he still qualify for a loan? There are many such cases of people who come here as students and then decide they would like to stay here. They are perfectly prepared to declare that they intend to stay here, but the immigration department frowns on this intention and will not permit them to stay.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: MEASURE TO FACILITATE MAKING LOANS TO STUDENTS
speechtext: I do not look upon that question as a frivolous one because I think there may be cases like this. Depending on the individuals and the circumstances, perhaps the immigration department might be so impressed with these students that they would feel they should be encouraged to stay. I do not know. There will not be very many such cases in the total and I fancy they will be taken care of in the ordinary way by the bodies that are set up to look into such matters.

subtopic: MEASURE TO FACILITATE MAKING LOANS TO STUDENTS
speechtext:
I think the hon. member for Greenwood has raised a very pertinent question. An increasing number of foreign students are coming to this country and we would like to attract them to our universities in increasing numbers. A condition of their 20220-369J
Loans to Students
admission to Canada, particularly from certain countries, is that they shall leave this country immediately upon completion of their studies. I think the minister is going to have to talk to his colleague, the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration, in this regard. We know that in so many instances they may come here to comply with the first year residence qualification that we require, and thereafter their funds get lower and lower. They are the ones who are taking jobs. All one has to do to see this is to visit some of the university towns. It is these people who are really in need of financial assistance. Yet I think something could be worked out for them in co-operation with the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: MEASURE TO FACILITATE MAKING LOANS TO STUDENTS
speechtext: I should perhaps explain that most of these students, especially the ones from Africa, come under various sponsored plans. There are a lot of other arrangements that take care of most of them. The reason the one year residence provision was inserted was that we really had in mind students from across the line who may come up here with this inducement.

subtopic: MEASURE TO FACILITATE MAKING LOANS TO STUDENTS
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, there are two points that bother me about this bill that I can argue from this particular clause. I do not believe there will be any difficulty within the provincial framework in students applying for loans for the normal university or advanced institutes, like the Nova Scotia technical institute or the Ryerson institute. However, I have the gravest doubts about how willing some of the provincial authorities may be, unless there is very strong encouragement, almost a memorandum of suggestion from the federal government, to permit students to take advantage of these loans to study outside the province. There is a certain selfishness involved in that many of the provinces, particularly Ontario, are putting a fair amount of money into the establishment of new universities. Many of these new universities are very anxious to expand their enrolment.
I would presume that the basic attitude on this bill is that if any young person in Ontario who is qualified to attend the university wants to go to McGill, say, rather than Trent or the Lakehead college or the University of Toronto, then there should be no impediment at all in his way to getting a loan to do that. It is for this reason I would like to hear more from the minister than he has told us about the kind of understanding or undertaking he has on these questions.

Loans to Students
The second point that bothers me was touched upon by the hon. member for York-Humber when he spoke on an earlier clause concerning specified educational institutions. It comes down to this: I should like to know why that phrase "post-secondary school level" could not have been spelled out more completely. I should like to give the minister two examples of citizens in my constituency who have encountered difficulty. One man discovered himself replaced as a clerical worker by a machine that Abitibi introduced into the clerical procedures.
He was a man in his thirties, and he wanted to go to normal school. He discovered that the national employment service was quite prepared to send him to various courses, but he could not get any support from the national employment service to permit him to complete his grade 13 which he needed in order to get into normal school. He did discover that there were some places in Canada that would be ready to take him in a university, on the first year level, with the qualifications he had, which were really an incomplete grade 12.
I know another young man who is about 24, married, with several children and he has discovered he has no occupational future in his particular line. He is trying to study at night in order to complete his senior matriculation to gain entrance into a university. Now, when you do not really spell it out but you just say "post-secondary school level", it seems to me this is going to lead to a certain amount of heartbreak in the future, as there are more and more older people trying to get back into the educational system in order to improve their qualifications.
This is the most hopeful thing in connection with this bill. It is not so much going to help the average young student, but so many of these people in their twenties and thirties who want to get back into the educational system in order to improve their qualifications, who have families to support and so on, to whom the loan is going to be particularly important. They cannot qualify under the normal arrangements. They do not go through the normal stream. In Ontario, now, we have four different streams going through the secondary schools. I do not want to go into the Robarts plan; but the minister knows what they are. It seems to me it is going to be manifestly unfair if this legislation aids people in the A stream who are going to enter university, because surely we cannot stop even at the next stream. It seems to me we have to be very liberal in the

interpretation of this phrase "post-secondary school level".
I want to say to the minister, and I am afraid it has been repeated here very often by our learned and humble legal friends, that the courts do not look at what politicians say in the House of Commons. I am also willing to make the point that provincial administrators who look at this bill will not pay too much attention to what we have said in this house. I should like to argue that the minister should give some more information as to the kind of understanding that he has had or that he is going to undertake to get from the provincial authorities.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: MEASURE TO FACILITATE MAKING LOANS TO STUDENTS
speechtext: In reply to the first point, Mr. Chairman, about students from one province who want to go to university in another, I may say that it was a new thought to me that Ontario universities, for example, were seriously beating the bushes for students.

subtopic: MEASURE TO FACILITATE MAKING LOANS TO STUDENTS
speechtext: I just want to say if the minister does not know they beat the bushes for students he has not been around the universities very much. You ask any graduate and you will find that McMaster and Queen's are awarding doctorates, and have for years, upon a selected basis in order to get recruiting going.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: MEASURE TO FACILITATE MAKING LOANS TO STUDENTS
speechtext:
I was associated with the board at Toronto university, and it seemed to me that they were doing just the opposite. However if they are beating the bushes for students, and if as a result of this bill prospective students are going to be able to get into university, I am pleased to hear it. My fear, and I think the fear of a good many other people, has been that there were not going to be enough university facilities to meet the demand.
However if a student in Ontario is not granted a certificate for a loan to go to the University of Manitoba, for example, all he has to do is apply to the loan board in Manitoba. There is no reason why he cannot do that.

subtopic: MEASURE TO FACILITATE MAKING LOANS TO STUDENTS
speechtext: It may be a little difficult.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: MEASURE TO FACILITATE MAKING LOANS TO STUDENTS
speechtext:
There is a difficult situation if he wants to go to McGill, as my hon. friend suggested, because Quebec will not be in the scheme and there will not be anybody to apply to.
In so far as post-secondary school level is concerned, or how you define it, I certainly agree with the hon. member for Port Arthur in the hope that a very liberal interpretation

of this is given by the authorities, the provincial bodies. It is certainly not intended to be restrictive. On the other hand, as we all know the criteria are different in the different provinces; in some provinces it is grade 12; in others it is grade 13, and there are some others where a student can enter a university with only a partial grade 12. If they are accepted, I cannot believe that they would not be entitled to a loan in that particular province. They may not be granted it in Ontario, but they could certainly apply in another province and receive it.
In so far as the four streams in Ontario high schools are concerned, it is certainly not intended that these loans should be restricted to those who go through the A stream, or whatever it is, the one that leads to an academic career.
It is certainly intended that this loan scheme should be available to the kind of people to whom the hon. member referred. We came to the conclusion that it was not a practical thing to try to spell out these criteria in detail. But if it is discovered from experience that people are being discriminated against or being left out, then I would have no hesitation in bringing in an appropriate amendment.

subtopic: MEASURE TO FACILITATE MAKING LOANS TO STUDENTS
speechtext:
I thank the minister for the strength of his last assurance. I want to add one or two other examples. I encounter a great many young people who are interested in going to the United States for courses of one year. Quite often they are not required to have anything superior in terms of qualifications. I think of a very well known school which is always advertised in the pulp magazines, or used to be-the Coyne school of electricity. I can also think of a number of diesel schools in the United States which have courses of longer than 26 weeks. I had a woman approach me not long ago, a hairdresser, and she wanted to take a long course in the United States to become what she called a beautician. It seems to me there is going to be a shadow. I do not know whether it is the purpose of this particular bill but I suggest that in the face of such a variety of opportunity, such a variety of attitudes, such searching for some kind of opportunity, we should not tend to be mesmerized by the more formal kinds of education offered by universities and institutes.
The last point I wish to make is something quite specific. It deals with the question of schools of chiropractic. In Ontario, chiropractors have been trying for some time to obtain recognition through a bill brought
Loans to Students
before the provincial legislature. To my knowledge, they have not made a great deal of progress in this direction, though in others they have. I have received a wire from the Ontario chiropractors asking me if I would make the point in this chamber that chiropractic should be one of the post-secondary school fields of education which would be recognized. I realize now, looking at the legislation, that this would be a decision for the provincial government to make. But I should like the minister to make a comment as to whether he feels this important kind of health training should be open for students to take advantage of through loans.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: MEASURE TO FACILITATE MAKING LOANS TO STUDENTS
speechtext:
I quite agree with that. In the course of this debate it has been said on many occasions that it may be far more important for many people to be trained in some vocation, some technical skill, rather than struggle to get perhaps a relatively inadequate B.A. The bill is certainly intended to cover those people. I agree with the hon. member that once you start to define who shall come under this scheme and who shall not, a considerable difficulty arises. I think the bodies which will be responsible for deciding, for instance, whether a course in some highly advertised business college or other in the United States should qualify for a loan under this act, will be under some obligation to decide whether that particular course is really worth the money or whether people are just going to be sucked in to pay fees and come out of it without very much benefit.
On the last point, another hon. member has spoken to me about chiropractors, and again all I can say is that I hope these provisions will be interpreted as generously as possible.

subtopic: MEASURE TO FACILITATE MAKING LOANS TO STUDENTS
speechtext: May I ask the hon. member for Port Arthur a question? Was his reference to hairdressing inspired by a glance at the noble heads of the hon. member for Edmonton West and the hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre?

subtopic: MEASURE TO FACILITATE MAKING LOANS TO STUDENTS
speechtext: No, it was not. I would also like to tell the hon. member that I, myself, am not inspired by the Beatles.

subtopic: MEASURE TO FACILITATE MAKING LOANS TO STUDENTS
speechtext:
I should like to direct my comments to the provision requiring residence of one year. I feel that one year is not sufficient time for a person to reside in Canada before he can take advantage of this far reaching and generous legislation to assist in providing higher education. Provision is also made that an applicant must declare he in-

Loans to Students
tends to reside in Canada. It seems to me that present residence in Canada is the very best guarantee of future intention. If a student is living in Canada and is a Canadian citizen, and if he has lived in Canada for two or three years, he is much more likely to continue living in Canada after he graduates than if he had been a resident of Canada for one year only; and I should like to suggest to the minister that he give this particular item further consideration and consider making the period of residence two or three years rather than one year.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: MEASURE TO FACILITATE MAKING LOANS TO STUDENTS
speechtext:
I appreciate the hon. member's remarks and the point he has made. I think that what we were afraid of when the bill was being drafted was that some bright child of a new immigrant, the sort of child who perhaps could benefit as much as anybody from higher education, would be prevented from obtaining it. We did not want to put a residence clause in here which would be so long as to make it impossible perhaps for some bright student of a new immigrant to qualify.
I think in practice there will be some other checks. In the first place, I doubt very much whether loans will be granted unless the provincial authorities are satisfied that those who apply really mean to take advantage of further education, and in this particular case that they intend to remain in Canada.

subtopic: MEASURE TO FACILITATE MAKING LOANS TO STUDENTS
speechtext: In that regard it seems to me that the provincial authorities will be expected to follow quite closely the provisions laid down in this bill. While naturally they will be expected to use discretion, if the bill says one year, then of course they would grant a certificate of eligibility on that basis. If it says two years or three years, it would be that much more of a brake on possible abuses of the legislation. This is very sweeping legislation and I think we had better go carefully first of all. Then if we find it is possible to ease the restrictions, that could be done in future. But it is much more difficult to impose additional restrictions. I certainly would like to see this particular provision extended to two or three years rather than one, because I believe it is rather dangerous.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General

subtopic: MEASURE TO FACILITATE MAKING LOANS TO STUDENTS
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, we did agree as a committee that the amendment would be introduced at this stage, but there was no agreement as to the substance of the amendment itself. It is to that matter that I wish to address my remarks. I made some, what I thought to be rather heroic efforts to have introduced the amendment that I knew was being proposed by the government, after having listened to the Solicitor General yesterday and after having read what he said in Hansard. But I do not believe the amendment goes far enough, and it is going to take me a few minutes to explain why.
Fundamentally the reason is that which was given by the hon. member for Greenwood when first proposing his amendment. It strikes at the constitutional machinery which has been set up for the government of the Yukon Territory in particular. The Northwest Territories, of course, have a different form of government and the form the amendment is now in would be acceptable, I believe, in so far as the Northwest Territories are concerned. As the minister knows, in the Northwest Territories there is a council of nine, four of whom are elected and five of whom are appointed. These appointees are selected and the appointments made by the governor in council, usually a function which is discharged by the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources. In the Yukon Territory, however, there is a wholly-elected council of seven, and the commissioner in all his functions of a legislative character acts only under and with the consent of that elected body.
In order that members might understand the substance of a subamendment which I am now forced to put before the committee, since my negotiations with the minister and other members on the government side have proven to be unfruitful, I will have to refer to the federal legislation which set up the

Loans to Students
office of the commissioner in the Yukon and the functions of the council in the Yukon.
I propose to put before the committee an amendment which will suggest that instead of the power residing only in the commissioner of the territory to appoint appropriate authorities, that power should reside in the commissioner acting either by and with the consent of, or in consultation with the advisory committee on finance, a body which was set up by amendment to the Yukon Act in 1960.
The powers of the commissioner and of the council are set out in the Revised Statutes of Canada, 1952-53. Those powers are broad enough to allow the commissioner and council to legislate on the same classes of subject matter as come within the purview and power of the legislatures of the provinces, with three exceptions. Those exceptions are: (1) natural resources, which come under the direct jurisdiction of the federal government; (2) the administration of justice, which comes under the direct administration of the federal government, the Minister of Justice being the Attorney General for the Yukon; and (3) that all money bills before they are introduced in the legislature of the Yukon must be introduced by the commissioner. In other words, a private member of the council of the Yukon cannot introduce a money bill. However before any moneys are expended from the consolidated revenue fund of the Yukon, before any civil servant is paid and before any contract is paid, the council must vote and approve the estimates in the same way and to the same extent that this committee of the whole must vote and approve every estimate of federal expenditure.
I realize that the provisions of this bill do not call for any direct expenditures by the provincial legislatures; but I believe I will find agreement when I suggest that the appropriate authority, once it has been set up by the lieutenant governor in council of a province and once it grants a certificate of eligibility to a student in need, is in effect authorizing the expenditure of $1,000 of federal funds.
It may be argued that the bank is the final arbiter here, since it may accept or reject an application by any student for a loan. But I suggest that this is a very shallow argument since the bank loan is guaranteed; and while the bank is going to exercise the prudence of ordinary business in granting or rejecting any loan, nonetheless it is going to be a telling factor that the loan is guaranteed by the federal government, and there will be very few loans, if any, which will be turned

down by the bank once an appropriate authority has granted that certificate of eligibility to a student.
The provisions of the Yukon Act to which I would like to refer the committee commence, for my purposes, at section 3, and I am going to read it into the record, because when hon. members of the committee have been sitting as a committee, as well as when they have been sitting in the house, they have heard me repeatedly direct questions to the government members on the treasury benches inferring that there is a lack of consultation with the governments of the Yukon Territory and the Northwest Territories when it comes to joint programs of a federal-provincial nature. Just this morning, while I know the minister of health is very concerned over the matter, we had yet another example of a piece of legislation which is supposed to operate on a joint basis, but where there had been absolutely no consultation with the governments of the two territories concerned.
Section 3 of the Yukon Act sets forth that-
-the governor in council may appoint for the territory a chief executive officer to be styled and known as the commissioner of the Yukon Territory.
In effect, while that power resides in the governor in council, again in practice it is the function of the minister of northern affairs to make that appointment and get the approval of his colleagues in the cabinet.
Section 4 sets out that-
-the commissioner shall administer the government of the territory under instructions from time to time given him by the governor in council or the minister.
In effect, the distinction which arises here between the government in the Yukon and that in a province is that the lieutenant governor in council in a province performs the executive function of government, whereas in the Yukon that executive function of government is performed by the commissioner on instructions from time to time given by the minister. In practice I know that a good deal of the time the commissioner exercises his own discretion in the hope that he will not embarrass whoever might be the minister of the day. But the power resides here and it is not uncommon to find the minister of northern affairs issuing directives to the commissioner to carry out that executive function of government.
You can see, Mr. Chairman, the situation which arises here with respect to this bill. The power existing for the appropriate authority to be appointed by the minister of

northern affairs; that is what it boils down to. The minister of northern affairs, by virtue of the powers given him under section 4 of the Yukon Act, can say to the commissioner, if the amendment in its restricted form is accepted by the committee, "This is going to be the appropriate authority", and the commissioner has no alternative but to follow the instructions of the minister in that regard.
This is precisely what the argument was all about on clause 2(b) of the bill, where all opposition parties have just finished voting to have the power of appointing these appropriate authorities reside in the governor in council. Here you are left with the situation where, if the amendment is accepted in its restricted form as put forward by the Minister of Industry on behalf of the Solicitor General, that is precisely what would happen: The governor in council, through the minister of northern affairs, is going to have the power under this bill to appoint the appropriate authority.
What strikes me as anomalous here is that the government-and the committee has decided rightly so-has decided to reside the power for the appointment of appropriate authorities in the lieutenant governors in council; in effect in the provincial cabinets. They are cabinets which are comprised of elected representatives of the people in those provinces. In order gradually to implement a plan for the growth of an autonomous and fully responsible form of government in the Yukon, an amendment was passed to the Yukon Act during the term of office of the previous government, which amendment will be found in the Yukon Act in the statutes of Canada, 1960. By that amendment an advisory committee on finance was set up. That is a committee which is chosen from among the elected representatives of the council and a committee with which the commissioner must consult when preparing his estimates for the expenditures for the forthcoming year. That amendment was passed with a view to providing the first stepping stone toward a fully responsible system of government in the Yukon, and toward commencing a gradual extraction of the complete and absolute powers of the commissioner and the minister from the bureaucracy-to use the term in a mild manner-and place it where it belongs, in the hands of the elected representatives of the people in the Yukon.
The principle of the amendment is a good one and I am sure the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources will agree 20220-370

with that. I am very happy to see him and his parliamentary secretary in their seats this afternoon listening to these submissions. They show an interest which the people of the Yukon expect and appreciate.
The legislative powers of the governor in council in the Yukon Territory are set forth in section 16 of the Yukon Act. If the parliamentary secretary to the Minister of Finance has studied section 16 of that act he knows it is almost on all fours with section 92 of the B.N.A. Act, and I shall select just at random a few of the subsections to substantiate further the point I am trying to make. Section 16 (a) gives the commissioner in council exclusive authority to legislate with respect to the-
-direct taxation within the territory in order to raise a revenue for territorial, municipal or local purposes.
That is the same wording as in the B.N.A. Act. Section 16 (b) gives the commissioner in council the power to set up a territorial civil service, which has been done and which has been operating for some years. Section 16 (r) gives the commissioner in council exclusive jurisdiction to legislate with respect to educational matters within the Yukon. More important than those I have just mentioned is section 16 (w) which sets forth that the commissioner in council has the exclusive authority to legislate with respect to-
-the expenditure of territorial funds and such portion of any moneys appropriated by parliament for the territory as the commissioner is authorized to expend by and with the advice of the council.
Here again you find a direct control of expenditures of a territorial and of a federal nature where it is so authorized by the elected representatives of the people. This is as it should be; this is right and proper. Yet the amendment in its existing restrictive form would now derogate from all of the progress made in this direction and place the power in the hands of one man, the commissioner, to designate the appropriate authority which in effect, by issuing the certificate of eligibility, is approving a loan of $1,000; and there is some $800,000 to be granted to the two territories under the provisions of this bill.
I would like to make a further point in this regard. The lieutenant governor of a province in the selection of the appropriate authorities in his province is I am sure going to pay very particular attention to the composition of any committees or boards set up as the appropriate authorities in the province. The cabinets of the provincial governments are

Loans to Students
going to have regard not only to geographical and other local factors but I am sure will have regard to religious factors, particularly in those provinces where there are separate school systems.
In the Yukon Territory there is a separate schools system. I am not suggesting for a moment that this will be the result-and it certainly will not be the result with the present incumbent of the office of commissioner in the Yukon, because he is one of the best commissioners the Yukon has ever enjoyed- but there could creep in an element of bias. If the commissioner wanted to, he could set up an appropriate authority which would be devoid of any representation by one particular religion or another. For instance, with the separate schools situation a commissioner could set up an appropriate authority without any Roman Catholic representation on that authority. On the other hand, if he happened to be a Roman Catholic commissioner he could set up an appropriate authority without any Protestant representation.
It is wrong to vest such power in the hands of one man. It is right that the elected representatives of the people, who are a cross section of all religious and ethnic groups, should share that power with the executive arm of government, and that is precisely the reason provincial cabinets are set up, and precisely the reason the government is placing this power in the hands of the lieutenant governors in council. I am sure the government would not have brought a bill before the committee which would have suggested that the power to appoint these appropriate authorities should be vested in the premier of a province or in any other one man. I believe the minister and the government would not want any doubt to arise with respect to the administration of the provisions of this act in complete impartiality, and I am sure if there is no harm in the principle I now espouse, that the minister, as he has previously indicated to me, would want to co-operate with the feelings, desires and wishes of the people of the Yukon and to allow them some say, through their elected representatives, as to the composition of the appropriate authority because after all, the students who will be benefitting in the Yukon, as elsewhere, from the provisions of this bill will come from every walk of life, will be of every religious and every ethnic group, and the broader representation you have in the composition of the appropriate authority the more insurance you have as to administrative impartiality.

Quite apart from the religious and other feelings of any particular commissioner at any particular time you will be constantly confronted with the situation, with power vested in one man whereby, even if the minister were to be so enlightened as to say to the commissioner that he wanted no part in making the decision as to who the appropriate authority was going to be, the minister could say to the commissioner, "These people are going to be your appropriate authority, and nobody else."
I am not suggesting for a moment that he is going to do that, but I am sure it will be agreed that he has that power; and it can be carried to the further logical and legal conclusion that the cabinet has that power. We in the Yukon Territory do not want in such cases to have that type of interference, and I suggest to the minister, and to the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources, that there can be no harm whatever in the minister's representative, the commissioner, at least going as far as to consult with the elected representatives of the people. Even if the commissioner is not obliged, by virtue of the amendment which I will be proposing, to obtain the consent of the council or of the advisory committee, at least he should be obliged to consult with them.
That does not detract from the power which resides in him, and in the minister ultimately, of making the decision regardless of the recommendation of the council or advisory committee. In 1960 that advisory committee was set up for the specific purpose of getting away from that autocratic and bureaucratic approach, and we are destroying the very intention of parliament by ignoring it now.
Therefore I would suggest, instead of the amendment that has been proposed in its restrictive form by the Minister of Industry, on behalf of the Solicitor General, that the following wording should be adopted:
That Bill C-110, an act to facilitate the making of loans to students, be amended by renumbering clause 2 as subclause (1) of clause 2 and by adding, immediately after subclause (1) of clause 2, the following subclause:
(2) In the application of this act to the Yukon Territory and the Northwest Territories, the expression "lieutenant governor in council" used in this act shall mean
(a)	in the case of the Yukon Territory, the commissioner of the Yukon Territory acting with the advice and consent of the advisory committee on finance;
(b)	in the case of the Northwest Territories, the commissioner of the Northwest Territories.
I think I should explain the reason for there being a difference between the two

territories in this regard. I have already explained that there exists a wholly elected council in the Yukon and I have already explained that by the act of 1960 amending the Yukon Act an advisory committee on finance was set up in the Yukon, a committee for the express purpose of reviewing the fiscal expenditures by the commissioner, reviewing his estimates and assisting him in the preparation of his estimates, a committee with which by the amendment of 1960 the commissioner is bound and obliged to consult. In the Northwest Territories where you have a preponderance of federally appointed members there is no such advisory committee, because it follows from the very construction of the Northwest Territories council that if it wishes the federal government can make all the decision anyway. But the very construction of the Northwest Territories council gives some indication of the desire of the federal government to hear the views of the elected representatives, because at least four of those on the Northwest Territories council are elected from among the people there. So 1 put forward this subamendment, seconded by the hon. member for Athabasca.
While the amendment is being distributed I might say that in paragraph (a) I have used words indicating that in the case of the Yukon Territory the expression "lieutenant governor in council" shall mean the commissioner of the Yukon Territory acting with the advice and consent of the advisory committee on finance, but as a happy compromise I would be willing to go so far as to suggest, if the government wishes to consider the altered wording favourably, that the words "in consultation with" be substituted for the words "with the advice and consent of". If the government does not want to go so far as to make the appointment of the appropriate authority the responsibility of the commissioner acting with the advice and consent of the advisory committee on finance, then at least the government should have no objection to the commissioner acting in consultation with the advisory committee composed of elected representatives of the people of the Yukon. Surely no harm could be done if the government were to accept that much. Surely no harm can be done if the commissioner consults with three of the elected representatives of the people of the Yukon before setting up this body, because if they go that far they are not impairing at all the powers of the commissioner since the commissioner, if he wishes to do so after consultation, can 20220-370J	.

I suggest it is consistent with democratic principles that the people of the Yukon Territory should be consulted in this and in other matters through their elected representatives and that it is wrong and invidious to continue a system of centralizing power in the hands of one man, no matter how enlightened that one person may be, when an alternative is open to the government which will ensure the right of the people of the Yukon to express their views on this type of matter and on other matters affecting their welfare.
