speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
subtopic: MEASURE TO FACILITATE MAKING LOANS TO STUDENTS
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I should like to reply briefly to the hon. member for Yukon and, with the greatest respect to the argument he has just made, urge the committee to reject the subamendment for these reasons. As I understand the division of powers set forth in the Yukon Act, administrative and executive power is exercised by the com-

Loans to Students
missioner who is responsible eventually to the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources, whereas legislative power is exercised by the commissioner in council, that is to say, the commissioner on the advice and with the consent of the elected council of the Yukon Territory.
In Bill No. C-110 now before the house the powers exercised by the lieutenant governor in council are administrative only and thus the equivalent, both within the meaning of the Yukon Act and within the meaning of the Northwest Territories Act, would be the commissioner acting alone subject to his eventual responsibility to the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources.
What the subamendment advanced by the hon. member for Yukon is in effect doing is mingling the legislative and executive powers as set forth in the Yukon Act and in effect constituting an amendment to the Yukon Act. I suggest to him that before such a measure could be adopted by the committee and eventually by the house it would have to have some mark of consent and approbation by the people of the Yukon as expressed by their own territorial representatives. If the balance as between executive and legislative power in the Yukon was to be changed by reason of this legislation, one would have thought that the people of the Yukon, expressing their opinion through their elected representatives, would have made some submission to this house. That has not been done.
The second reason why I would urge the committee to reject the subamendment is that it would have the commissioner acting with the advice and consent of the advisory committee on finance.
Now, the hon. member for Yukon, it is true, suggested a happy compromise, and I use his words. He said he would be willing to have the commissioner for the Yukon act in consultation with the advisory committee on finance. He pointed out that the advisory committee on finance was set up under the 1960 amendment to the Yukon Act. The form of consultation set forth in subsection (3) of section 12 is as follows:
The commissioner shall consult with the committee in the preparation of the estimates of the expenditures and appropriations required to defray the charges and expenses of the public services of the territory for each fiscal year.
In other words, this advisory committee on finance is a committee which the commissioner must consult on the matter of estimates and future expenditures. Despite the arguments adduced by the hon. member for Yukon, there is nothing in this bill giving
[Mr. Turner. 1
the lieutenant governor in council, and thereby the commissioner for the Yukon or the commissioner for the Northwest Territories, any discretion over expenditures or estimates. Clause 2(b) refers merely to the designation of the appropriate authority and clauses 10 and 11 have to do with the issuance of certificates and the eligibility of students.
Now, once the certificate has been issued, once the appropriate authority has been selected, then the expenditure of money is made through a bank, subject to a guarantee by the federal government. The advisory committee to the commissioner for the Yukon, therefore, would be acting beyond its functions because it would not be dealing with expenditures or estimates as contemplated under the amendment to the Yukon Act. In effect, what the hon. member for Yukon is asking us to do by this amendment is to change the functions of the advisory committee on finance from one of consultation on estimates and expenditures into one of acting as a joint authority with the commissioner over education.
Surely this would constitute an indirect type of legislation over education. The hon. member for the Yukon himself has said that the Yukon Act, section 16(r), stated that the commissioner and council may legislate for education in the territory. At the same time he asks us, by reason of this amendment, to enact such a legislative provision to change the function of the advisory committee on finance into an advisory committee on education.
I would submit finally that the committee, within the terms of the amendment to the Yukon Act of 1960, is an advisory committee on finance and, as presently constituted, would not have the power to act in accordance with the additional power the hon. member for Yukon would give it by way of his subamendment. I emphasize very strongly that what he says by way of a base for his argument indicates he is looking forward to a greater degree of responsible government for the Yukon and looking forward eventually to the day, as we all are, when the territory will have provincial status. However, this type of redressing of the balance between the executive and legislative power that would give final and full control within section 92 of the British North America Act to the Yukon as a province, surely would have to be done by way of amendment to the Yukon Act instead of by way of a rider to this type of legislation now before the committee. I feel that the commissioner in any event, when faced with this legislation,

if and when adopted by this committee, would want to consult with the people of the Yukon and the terms of the subamendment would unduly restrict him as to those with whom he should consult.
The hon. member for the Yukon mentioned the problem of religious affiliation. If we were to accept his argument, and if the advisory committee were to be consulted by the commissioner, then the advisory committee on finance itself would have to be based on religious affiliation. For these reasons, Mr. Chairman, I would urge the committee to reject the subamendment proposed by the hon. member for Yukon.

All I have suggested in the subamendment is that the commissioner, in whom the amendment proposes shall reside the power of appointing an appropriate authority shall, before he makes that appointment, consult with the advisory committee on finance or, if you wish, consult with the council elected, the representatives of the people. This is all the subamendment suggests. I think it is wrong to continue allowing the power to reside in the hands of one appointed executive when it need not be continued. I think that the parliamentary secretary, in his attempt to rebut the arguments which I have made-and while I will give him full marks for effort, it did not come close to dealing with the substance of it-has missed entirely the point that I made that the commissioner, by section 4 of the Yukon Act, must administer the territory from time to time on the instructions of the minister of northern affairs.
In reality, you have a situation where the minister of northern affairs has the power to instruct the commissioner as to what is going to be done to constitute the appropriate authority. The minister of northern affairs has authority to say to the commissioner, "You will be the appropriate authority". He has authority to say, "Mr. Commissioner, you and your council will be the appropriate authority", or he has power to say, "You are not going to make any decision on this until it is approved by me". I am not for a moment suggesting the minister of northern affairs would do that. I am suggesting that that situation is wrong and that the people who are most concerned are the parents of students in the Yukon, just as they are in the provinces, and the people of the Yukon themselves.
Surely, there can be nothing wrong with requiring the commissioner, before he makes a decision as to who is going to constitute the appropriate authority, to consult with all or some of the elected representatives of the people in the territorial council. What is so hideous about such a suggestion? Surely, the whole purpose of a democracy is to hear the views of the people instead of the views of the bureaucracy-again, I use the word in a mild sense. Is not this the idea of democracy, that instead of having the administration make all the decisions, those decisions should be subject to some sort of review by

the elected people of this country? What is wrong with having the commissioner consult with the elected representatives of the people? Surely there can be nothing unacceptable about such a suggestion.
As I have said, I am prepared to accept an alteration of the subamendment I put forward, though I think some members of the territorial council would not be too happy with this suggestion, neither would a good many people who live in the northwest. But if the government does not wish to accept the phrase "acting with the advice and consent of the committee", then in order to introduce this principle of consultation with the elected council, I would agree that the words might be substituted by a requirement that the commissioner should at least consult with the advisory committee.
The parliamentary secretary says that to accept such an amendment as I have proposed would be to usurp the functions of the amendment of 1960 which set up the committee, but in saying that he is away off base. The whole intention behind passing that amendment in 1960 was to take a first step towards eventual fully responsible government in the territories. It would not be a usurpation of the powers granted to that committee which, in effect, are no powers at all-all it has is the power to require to be consulted in the preparation of estimates. It would be no usurpation of the functions of that committee to be used as a sounding board of the opinions of the elected representatives of the people of the Yukon and that is all I am suggesting here.
If the government does not wish to accept the words "advice and consent", then at least let them accept the words "in consultation with." I would point this out to the minister, that even if the advisory committee were to say "We want a, b, and c, appointed to the proper authority" the minister could still say "Well, I do not want to accept your advice and I shall appoint x, y, and z". All I am requesting is that the commissioner should consult with the representatives of the people of the Yukon through their council, and surely that is not too much to expect.
I am grateful to the minister and to his advisers for bringing in the amendment in its existing form because it shows a certain co-operation which I am sure I appreciate and the people I represent appreciate. I am sure my arguments have gotten through to the Minister of Finance even if they have not gotten through to the parliamentary secretary to the minister of northern affairs. It is not

a question here of relying on technical arguments: It is a fundamental and basic matter. All the people of the Yukon want is the right to be consulted.

That is why I find quite reasonable the last suggestion made by the hon. member for Yukon to the effect that the commissioner for the Yukon Territory should be mentioned after consultation with the elected representatives of the Yukon.

I think that the last suggestion of the hon. member for Yukon is a reasonable one, but it could be slightly changed. It would then read as follows:
In this act, lieutenant governor in council means the commissioner of the Yukon Territory or the Northwest Territories after consultation with the elected representatives of the Yukon Territory or the Northwest Territories, as the case may be.
